extracted.intended_audience: general readers and researchers interested in historical cryptography, psychical research (crystal-gazing), botany (Cryptomeria), and crystallography
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted encyclopedia entries covering methods and practical guidance for deciphering ciphers, conducting crystal-gazing experiments, cultivation of Cryptomeria, and laboratory/observational details of crystallization and crystallography. The page is a multi-topic reference (encyclopaedic) rather than a single-procedure manual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency-analysis and common-word heuristics for deciphering transposition ciphers
rubrics_metrics.description: The decipherer's first business is to classify the letters of the secret message in the order of their frequency. The letter that occurs oftest is e; and the next in order of frequency is t.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a recommended letter-frequency order (roughly): e, t; then a, o, n, i; r, s, h; d, l; c, w, u, m; f, y, g, p, b; v, k; x, q, j, z. All single letters must be a, I or O. Common double letters: ee, oo, ff, ll, ss, &c. Common two-letter English words (roughly in order): of, to, in, it, is, be, he, by, or, as, at, an, so, &c. Common three-letter words: the and (in great excess), for, are, but, all, not, &c. Common four-letter words: that, with, from, have, this, they, &c. Familiarity with language composition and reference to Poe's "The Gold Bug" are suggested for additional hints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word-based (dictionary) codes used for telegraph and secrecy
rubrics_metrics.description: Codes constructed on the basis of words: classified words taken from dictionaries being made to represent complete ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that such word-codes have been adapted for telegraph to keep business private and to reduce cost; they present greater difficulties to the decipherer than simple letter-substitution/transposition systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of figures, numerals and arbitrary characters in ciphers
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures and other characters have been also used as letters; with them ranges of numerals have been combined as the representatives of syllables, parts of words, words themselves, and complete phrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples (e.g., complex numeral cipher of Charles I deciphered by Wheatstone) show these systems can be highly elaborate. Such ciphers often require catalogued keys and specific expertise (see referenced treatises) to decipher.

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques for increasing cipher security: nulls, false divisions and keyed tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Complications have been introduced into ciphers by the employment of 'dummy' letters--'nulls and insignificants.' Other devices: spelling words backwards, making false divisions between words, &c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States the greatest security has been found in the use of elaborate tables of letters arranged in the form of the multiplication table, the message being constructed by the aid of preconcerted key-words. These devices are intended to perplex the decipherer and make decryption one of the most difficult tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural method for scrying (crystal-gazing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The usual method: place a glass ball on a dark ground, sit with the back to the light, focus the gaze on the ball (disregarding reflections if these cannot be excluded), and await results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical details: perhaps five to ten minutes is a long enough time for the experiment. The scryer may let consciousness play freely and should not be disturbed by lookers-on. If a person has the faculty they 'see' at the first attempt; if they fail in the first three or four efforts they need not persevere. Solitude is advisable at first. Objects used vary widely (crystal, ink, mirror, water, liver, etc.); different seers have preferences. The writer reports scryers retain normal consciousness (no trance) in his experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental controls and recommended protocol for scientific study of scrying
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendations for how experiments should be conducted to avoid bias and suggestion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not tell the scryer more than that he is to descry the inquirer's thoughts; there ought never to be physical contact (e.g., holding hands) between inquirer and scryer during the experiment. Avoid using hysterical or professionally visionary subjects whose testimony is unreliable. Keep careful, attested records and have experiments conducted by investigators ('savants') of recognized standing. Avoid paid professionals who might lead subjects to error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretive cautions and research needs for scrying results
rubrics_metrics.description: On interpretation: crystal visions may resemble hypnagogic illusions or visualization but sometimes appear to include 'supra-normal' or telepathic/clairvoyant elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author urges restraint: do not rush to metaphysical hypotheses; what is needed is 'a large, carefully tested, and well-recorded collection of examples, made by savants of recognized standing.' Anecdotes alone are insufficient; experiments should be well-attested and designed to distinguish imagination, telepathy, and possible clairvoyance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivation requirements and uses of Cryptomeria japonica (Japanese cedar)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cryptomeria is extensively used in Japan for reafforesting denuded lands and for avenues; many varieties exist including dwarfs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When grown in Great Britain Cryptomeria requires a deep, well-drained soil with plenty of moisture, and protection from cold winds. Notes on height (100+ ft in native settings) and ornamental use (avenues, temple groves) are provided as context for planting decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laboratory and practical techniques for crystallization
rubrics_metrics.description: Crystallization: to obtain a substance in the form of crystals, typically by exploiting solubility differences with temperature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General best-practices: use a boiling concentrated solution and allow it to cool; the slower the cooling the larger and more perfect the crystals. If a solution refuses to crystallize, inoculate with a minute crystal of the same or similar substance, shake the solution, or add a drop of another solvent. 'Fractional crystallization' consists in repeatedly crystallizing a salt to separate substances of different solubilities (useful in separating rare-earths). Other formation modes (from fused mass or vapour) are noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core topics and structure for study or exposition in crystallography
rubrics_metrics.description: Outline of principal sections and topics to be addressed in crystallography.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a topical syllabus: I. Crystalline form (a. symmetry of crystals; b. simple forms and combinations; c. law of rational indices; d. zones; e. projection and drawing; f. crystal systems and classes (cubic, tetragonal, orthorhombic, monoclinic, anorthic, hexagonal); g. regular grouping/twinning; h. irregularities of growth; i. theories of crystal structure). II. Physical properties of crystals (elasticity/cohesion, optical properties, thermal properties, magnetic/electrical properties). III. Relations between crystalline form and chemical composition. This serves as guidance for what aspects to cover in a rigorous treatment of crystallography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Microscopic identification and characteristics of crystallites and microliths
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions and distinguishing features in viscous/rapidly-cooled media: crystallites are rudimentary or imperfect forms occurring in an amorphous glassy base; microliths have crystalline properties and belong to definite minerals or salts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes observable forms and behaviour: globulites (spherical non-crystalline), margaritic strings, globospherites, longulites, baculites, trichites; microliths present as thin fibres, short prisms, rods or equidimensional grains depending on mineral (examples: felspar, augite, enstatite, magnetite). Notes about growth patterns (e.g., prisms with funnel-shaped ends filled with vitreous material), tendency to form spherulites or skeletal crystals, and relations between microliths and larger porphyritic crystals. Useful for microscopic identification and interpretation of textural origins.
